utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Can we have the case called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I notice, General Talic, that again we are back to square one. We don't have either Maitre Pitron or Maitre de Roux. Are you still happy with the situation? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Yes. For this week, that's what we have agreed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The usual, Joanna Korner, assisted by Susan Grogan. Good morning Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your [Realtime transcript read in error "Honour"] Honours. I'm John Ackerman, I'm with Tanja Radosavljevic and Milan Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearance for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau, assisted by Fabien Masson. I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam . And good morning to you. So -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a slight correction in the transcript. When I said good morning. I said good morning Your Honours. Meaning I said good morning to all three of you. And the transcript only says I said good morning to you, Your Honour. And I wouldn't want to leave the other two judges out. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes, could one help Madam Fauveau, please. Usher. Yes, Judge. Now, good morning to you. Could I ask you to repeat the solemn declaration once more before you start giving evidence today, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. So what's going to happen, Judge, today is Madam Fauveau will conclude presumably her cross-examination, and then Mr. Ackerman will commence his. Mr. Ackerman, as I told you before, is counsel for -- lead counsel for Radoslav Brdjanin. Yes, Madam Fauveau. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 26th of April, you spoke about General Talic's visit to the Manjaca camp. On page 5084 of the French transcript. Why didn't you mention General Talic's visit to the Manjaca camp in any of your written statements?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it seems to you that you saw General Talic at the observation post. What was the distance between you and this observation post?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 metres to 80 metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that you were mistaken and that you didn't see General Talic but someone else?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said -- and it's still on the 26th of April, 2002, page 5087 -- when counting all the persons who died in Manjaca and those who died in the transport, there were between 60 and 80 persons who died. Could you say how many people died in the Manjaca camp itself?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for what I saw with my very own eyes, I saw eight people being killed in front of the entrance; that is to say, by the gate. That's when the transport arrived from Prijedor in the morning, when people were being taken off the buses. I saw these eight people being killed. In the camp, as far as I know, four persons were killed and then one died as a consequence of the beatings, so that's five. I think that one or two died -- I don't know -- from an illness or the consequences of hunger. I know that one man from the village of Crljeni from the municipality of Kljuc died two days before a transport was supposed to go to England transporting the ill. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the death of Omer Filipovic. Did you see his body?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see this body?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it as they were carrying him out of the horse stables in the morning, when there was some military commission that was carrying out an investigation and when the body was held there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about an incident in which about 20 people died. They suffocated in transport on the way to Manjaca. Did you personally see their bodies?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see their bodies myself, but I spoke about that. I said how I found out about this event that night and also the next days, the following days we talked about this at the camp and we knew what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that the representative of the Red Cross went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to the representative of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, several times at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of speaking to the representative of the International Red Cross without the guards being present?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 13th of May -- it's page 12 of the LiveNote -- you said that there was only one exchange of prisoners. Could you be more precise and say which exchange you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what I know, this was an exchange that took place on the 14th of November, 1992 at Vlasic. Once this exchange didn't go through, but the next time it succeeded. This was an exchange of civilians from the camp for combatants, as far as I managed to find out -- Serb combatants.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether an exchange took place on the 25th of June?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about an exchange that took place on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was organised, but I don't know whether it was carried out actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about another exchange on the 28th of July?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about an exchange that took place on the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of August?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of exchange was this and where? I don't know. It's not that people went from Manjaca, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, are you aware of a particular date when an exchange as the one that is being suggested to you took place? At least the month.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the 14th of November. That's when there was an exchange and when it actually went through. Several times there were attempts to have an exchange, but people were returned to the camp. I don't know. Possibly there was one more exchange at Jajce, but I really don't know about that. Perhaps this took place before I was released from solitary confinement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are not aware of any other exchanges that may have taken place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So please, next question, because we can't go on from one week -- or from one month to the other, when you could ask a simple, direct question. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that there were regular exchanges of which you were not aware?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay at the camp, I could notice if somebody went to be exchanged. In July, August, September, October. Perhaps there were some individual cases. People went perhaps on an individual basis for money. I know of some individual cases of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that may be a good point -- is it suggested that these were large-scale exchanges? In other words, more than a few individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The suggestion is -- the suggestion is that there were regular exchanges but not on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about people who had been released from Manjaca. Could you confirm that the persons who were elderly and underage people were released from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that elderly people from the municipality of Sanski Most were released. That happened once.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that through the intermediary of the International Red Cross, a group of persons was sent to England from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that a certain number of clerics were also released from Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember about a particular number. But they were released quite late. They spent a long time in Manjaca, in the camp of Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm that the Merhamet representatives visited Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you say, Madam Fauveau, a representative in the singular or the plural? Because here the translation -- the interpretation says "Merhamet representative," just one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "the representatives," in the plural?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I have confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to read to you a report from an international organisation. And for the record, it's document 763, which was communicated in accordance with Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. 763?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Am I right --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Madam Fauveau spoke to me about this, and I said there was no objection by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a confidential document, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was dealt with, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I -- Your Honour, I have no objection to it being -- part of it being put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the first paragraph on page 3, the second sentence. I'm going to read this part of the report which dates from the 23rd of June, 1992. And I'm going to ask you whether you agree with this analysis of the Manjaca camp. [In English] "The delegation from Merhamet visited a prisoner camp at Manjaca mountain where 1.200 persons are held by the army. Material conditions were poor, especially concerning hygiene. But there were no signs of maltreatment or execution of prisoners, they reported."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please see this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I can't show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can be shown the paragraph in question, just the paragraph. It's on page 3, at the top of the page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You object?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do. I'm sorry. This -- all that the witness is being asked to do -- and I appreciate he wants to see the document -- is does he agree that's an accurate description of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will read it out to you, Judge. The Prosecution has every right to object to this, because this is a confidential document released to the Prosecution under a special -- I'm going to read out to you very clearly the paragraph in question, which is -- forms part of a report which is dated 23rd of June, 1992 and covers the period 16 to 20th of June, 1992 and updated on the 22nd -- being an update on the situation as it was obtaining previously on the 22nd of May, 1992 till 16th of June, 1992. So basically we have an update of the situation relating to the dates 16th to 20th June, 1992, even though the report is dated 23rd of June. The paragraph in question reads as follows: "Arbitrary detention of persons allegedly participating or planning hostile actions against Serbian authorities." These last words are in quotes. "A delegation from Merhamet visited a prisoner camp at Manjaca mountain where 1.200 persons are held by the army. Material conditions were poor, especially concerning hygiene, but there were no signs of maltreatment or execution of prisoners, they reported." And then there is another part of the paragraph which does not concern us. So this is the report. And this is supposedly a report by an independent observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need to -- I need to make it clear that it's someone reporting what supposedly Merhamet --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Reported to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reported to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it's not an independent observer of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What -- who is reporting this is an independent observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's reporting or she's reporting not just -- not to give an indication -- what supposedly Merhamet representatives who had visited Manjaca camp had reported to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I think the simple question that Madam Fauveau asked was: Does he agree that that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Do you agree that as on 16th to 20th of June, 1992, the description of the conditions in Manjaca, as I read out to you, is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree with that. That has no foundation whatsoever. Merhamet was under the control of the Serbian authorities. And those people who wrote that, they should be ashamed of that. At the time it was terrible in the camp. There was beating, maltreatment, and other things, killing. I've already spoken about this -- returning people who had disappeared in the transport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's shameful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were 5.434 prisoners. How did you get this figure? 5.434 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say 7.000. I said 5.434. That's the number of people who went through the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. According to the interpretation that I am receiving, at least, I don't think you said 7.000, did you? Here I have 5.434. And Madam Fauveau wants to know how you came up to that figure. What's the basis of your information, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This information is reliable. I obtained this information, this accurate information, on the basis of the statement of a camp inmate, Ibrahim Begovic is his name, and he kept records. He was at the other camp. He is perfectly aware of that figure. I agree with that figure, because my estimation was about 6.000 -- my estimate was about 6.000, so I know exactly how many people were in one camp and how many people were in the other camp. So at the time when the inmates from Omarska, Sanski Most, and other places arrived, there were about 4.500. So one camp, about 2.000, 2.250, and about that many in the other one. These are approximately accurate figures. And as for that particular figure, I got it from the statement of an inmate who kept records. So the figure is 5.434. That is from the 1st of June until the 18th of December, 1992. That's how many people went through the camp. That's how many people were deprived of all conceivable rights, all human rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that this figure is not exact and that the total number of detainees in Manjaca was 4.400, more or less?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure ranging between 4.400 to 4.500 refer to the summer period; that is to say, when people arrived from Sanski Most and Prijedor, when they were transported. I know that for sure because I was cutting bread, and I know how many slices of bread I had to cut. And also, I took cards -- International Red Cross cards when I was cutting bread, so I knew exactly how many people there were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look at an extract from a videotape. It's a videotape that the Prosecutor has already shown you. I'm not going to show the entire tape but just the part where Paddy Ashdown made a comment on leaving the camp. And I'm going to ask you to read the subtitles, since there are Serbo-Croat subtitles. I'd like you to read what Paddy Ashdown said as he was leaving the camp. It's Prosecutor's document 468 -- P468. Sir, can you read the subtitles in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Judge, please let me decide. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, Your Honour. "When leaving, he stated that no matter how dismal things looked --"

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next sequence.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It seems that this camp was run properly."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This cassette dates back to August 1992. Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a person's very own opinion based on one particular thing that was seen. I do not agree with this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about an exhumation which took place in the year 2000 and at which you found the body of your colleague Nedzad Muhic. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned that. I mentioned they saw the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say where the location was of this mass grave, the mass grave in which Nedzad Muhic was found?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Krkojevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this mass grave in the vicinity of a bank -- of a river bank?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's different, between a bank and a river bank. Yes, okay. But for a moment I thought what does a bank have -- what does it have to do with it -- with the mass grave. It's a river bank we are talking about, not a bank, because the translation here said a bank, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There are no buildings there. This is the canyon of the Sana River.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And Nedzad Muhic was allegedly killed in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say how you recognised Nedzad Muhic's body in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the clothes he was wearing, because we were in prison together. We were together in prison at the public security station, and I know what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P778. It's in fact the map that is over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the map that we had yesterday, which I see in the back there. It's still there. Judge, if you need to stand up at any time, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay, usher. Usher, it's okay. Yes. It's -- wait for the question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you found this map in 1995 in the house of the Nezirevic family in Sanski Most; is that correct? Did you yourself find this map?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and I'm the one who found this map. I'm the one who took it from this house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you find this map?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I found this map in the second half of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find this map accidentally, or were you aware of the fact that there were military documents in that house?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my street where my burnt house was, in Mahala. And this house is about 150 to 200 metres away. That's where the primary school in Mahala is. The command of the brigade was in this primary school during that period; that is to say, that the military command was there and the military police of the 6th Krajina Brigade. And I toured these buildings. This house was also burnt down, and I knew that it was repaired during the war and that meetings were held there. It's like a villa by the river. That's where there were some documents, and I took them over, maps for the most part, including this one. This was in the basement of that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So before going to that house, you found -- where you found that map, you knew or you assumed that you would be able to find military documents there. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone able to enter that house before you arrived and before the Serbs left Sanski Most, and would such a person have been in a position to place that map there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why anybody would do that. When I came, there were some military people there in Sanski Most -- or rather, operations were still taking place towards Banja Luka and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this map is titled, "The war route of the 6th Brigade"?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says, "The war journey of the 6th Krajina Brigade." It means the same thing, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this term, "the war route, war journey," and answer the question only if you know the answer -- is it true that this term is only used when a state of war has been declared?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with what you stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it the term that a military person would have used for the situation which existed in the Republika Srpska in 1992 and 1993? Wouldn't such a person have used the term "the combat route," rather than "the war route"?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your statement, because I found other documents too, such as, for example, the manuscript of the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Colonel Branko Basara. And he is describing their war route, their war journey in this report. And this was submitted to the Prosecution, the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as these manuscripts are concerned belonging to Colonel Basara, how do you know that they belonged to Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know? This is a leading question, but I shall respond nevertheless. His signature is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, Judge, Judge. I don't know what the system is in your country, but over here on cross-examination you can be asked direct questions, leading questions. So please -- and I frankly don't see the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But it's a simple question. You're making an allegation, a statement, that these documents belonged to Colonel Basara or -- you're being asked to explain how you know that or how you came to that conclusion. So what's wrong with that question? It's a perfectly legitimate one. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of his signature, handwriting, and the facts presented in that report, and the place where the document was found, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How can you affirm that this document was really written by Basara?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I affirm that? I said it on the basis of his handwriting, his signature, and the place where the document was found, and the facts that are mentioned. This document was not something that was observed here in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Basara left Sanski Most in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when he left. On the basis of the documents and analyses that I had. But I know that he did leave Sanski Most and that another commander was appointed. I think it was Mr. Kajtez.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll return to the map. Could you have a look at what is written next to "Bosanski Brod."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, if you need to leave your place to have a closer look, please do. But then when you speak, do speak -- do go back to your place and speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it says "Bosanski Brod," and that there is a date next to that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It says "Bosanski Brod," and there is an arrow towards Bosanski Brod and also there is a date, the 18th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this town, Bosanski Brod, was called Srpski Brod in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we know from when it is said that Bosanski Brod was called Srpski Brod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think some other witness did mention that. I can't remember exactly who. But he did give that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't recall the date, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking Madam Fauveau if she'd be kind enough to suggest from what date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, please. I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I know, immediately after the Serbian army arrived in Bosanski Brod, this town was renamed Srpski Brod; that is to say, in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This map dates back to May 1993 at the earliest, because the last mark on this map is May 1993. Why would the Serbs have used the name of Bosanski Brod for a town which they themselves had renamed Srpski Brod?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that a war route or a combat route should show the exact movements of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that. That is precisely what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this map, the 6th Brigade went to Srebrenica and Bratunac and it went through -- it passed through Travnik. Could you explain how a Serbian brigade could have passed through Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this shows the municipalities, the territories or the municipalities. That's where the arrow is pointing. It's not pointing towards the town itself, because the 6th Krajina Brigade was at Vlasic, the territory of Travnik, that is. And it took part in operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at the war route of the 6th Brigade in the direction of Bratunac, the 6th Brigade would have had to pass through territory under the control of Muslims. How could it have done such a thing?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, because this brigade had corridors -- or rather, up to Bratunac, the territory was linked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But I agree with you on that point, sir. But the arrow on the map passes through Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrow does not necessarily depict the direction of movement. It just shows the territory of the municipalities where the brigade operated. This is a map. And the arrows do show the municipalities where the brigade was and where it operated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But five minutes ago or even less you said that a war route should show the exact movements of a brigade. So if this map is authentic, it would have shown the real route that the brigade took to reach Bratunac; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's right. Military experts know where they went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a military map or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a military map.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why would members of the military have made a map that didn't correspond to the military route?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert for maps or a military expert, so I can't really answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that this map was made by anyone but a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would anybody else chart a map except for the military, except for the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The 6th Krajina Brigade in May 1993 allegedly used the name Bosanski Brod for a town called Srpski Brod and allegedly showed a route which wasn't the real route. Can one call that the war route?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are official names of municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina; therefore, I believe that this is an official map, a military map, of the 6th Krajina Brigade where they show the territories where they were at the front line. There are also other documents and reports. Believe me. In Sanski Most, we found this military documentation. It says exactly when people left, on which buses, and how many people, and the exact names and surnames of the people involved. So there are other documents too that show this. This is not the only document. General Talic will agree with me, won't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has said that these names -- the official names of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since when has the army of Republika Srpska respected the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than the laws of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I have no answer to that question of yours. I don't know how to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question once more, and then I will move on to another subject. Would you allow for the possibility that this map was not made by members of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not allow for that possibility. This map was made by the members of the 6th Krajina Brigade. And it's in colour too, the original, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness document P667.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a list of persons who were arrested between the 18th of May and the 6th of June, 1992 in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of civilians collected from the houses of Sanski Most. They are Bosniaks and Croats. They're no prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who found this document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document came from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you find this document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the public security station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document bear a signature?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a stamp on the document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a date on the document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a date. It says "List from the 18th of May until the 16th of June. Persons handed over to the military investigation authorities of the 5th Corps for further investigation procedure." And this is from a file of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The dates that you have just mentioned, it's in fact the period during which these persons were arrested. That's correct, isn't it? It's not the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was compiled in that period. That is my assertion. My name is in this document too, under number 85. And from the public security station -- from the prison, my name was called out and I was taken out and transported by a truck on the 17th of June. I know all these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the dates that you have read, the 18th of May and the 6th of June, they refer to the period during which these people were arrested; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that these persons were not taken prisoner. They were arrested or called in for an interview, an interrogation, and then they were kept in prison. But they were not taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what interpretation you received in Serbo-Croat, what the translation was in Serbo-Croat, but the verb "arreter" in French means arrest. So could you answer my question. Were these people arrested during the period 18th of May, 6th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But this document doesn't have a date. The document itself hasn't been dated. We don't know when this document was written.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no date on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document could have been written on the 6th of June at the earliest?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say, because the inspectors of the crime investigation service in Sanski Most, when they actually processed this document and when they brought this to Manjaca, I really don't know, because there should be a document of this kind in Manjaca when they came up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since the people mentioned in this document were arrested between the 18th of May and the 6th of June, do you agree that this document could not have been written before the 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrest started on the 25th of May, and I don't know when this document was made but I know when these people were arrested, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you a document which didn't have a signature and didn't have a stamp. You said that it wasn't an official document. In that case, why -- why is this document without a signature, without a stamp, without a date? Why would this document be an official document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document -- well, you can take it as an unofficial document too, but it does show something. Facts are contained in it, facts, and a list of persons who were arrested and handed over to the 5th Corps of the Yugoslav army for further investigation procedure. And thank God most of these people are still alive. They will say when they were arrested and when they were detained and when they were at Manjaca and when they were released and what they lived through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You allow for the possibility that it's not an official document.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an official document; that is to say, from the documentation of the public security station in Sanski Most, from the official file of investigators. And it is the way -- it was taken over from the public security station. It's in the same file, the same binder. This is the original, and that's the way it's been since then, and I still stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 6th of June, 1992 the 5th Corps no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say the 6th or the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because again we've got the 6th Corps. Now, it's the 5th Corps, Judge, not the 6th. I don't know what interpretation you got.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This shows that the document was made earlier -- that is to say, during the arrest of people and while they were being investigated, interrogated. I know that the 5th Corps was transformed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. You said that the first arrest took place on the 25th of May. Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 25th of May, the 5th Corps no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date exactly when the 5th Corps of the JNA was transformed into the 1st Krajina Corps of the Serb army. I can't remember the exact date. But it's not important what it says up here. I know who did this. I know who arrested us. I know who escorted us, who -- I know where we were, and I know who was responsible for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But that's another problem. What I'm interested in at the moment is the authenticity of this document. And I can understand very well that you don't know when the 5th Corps withdrew from Bosnia. But it seems to me nevertheless that an officer from the Sanski Most police station would have known that the 5th Corps was no longer in existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... but not to give her own interpretation of what a police officer knew in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She's right, Madam Fauveau. Ms. Korner is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll reformulate that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- and if you don't, just say that you don't know the answer -- do you know why a person who was allegedly an official of the Serbian state -- why would such a person who said that these people were forwarded to the 5th Corps -- were handed over to the 5th Corps since this corps was no longer in existence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what kind of a Serb state? What kind of a Serb state are you talking about? This is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the Serbian state was not in existence, that the Republika Srpska did not exist?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure what the answer was. Could the witness please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, could you repeat your answer, because the interpreters did not quite get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, what kind of a Serb state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But the question was: "Do you mean to say that the Serbian state was not in existence, that Republika Srpska did not exist?" This was the question. And you answered something which the interpreters did not hear well. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said what she says is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could translate that for you. The witness said that what I am saying is rubbish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam Fauveau, please. And Judge, as a Judge I think don't put me in a position where I have to explain to you that you have no right to attribute the kind of statements to Defence counsel, who are only doing their duty here. I'm sure that if you were in my position, you'd be doing exactly the same. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me how an official of the Serbian state or of Republika Srpska, if you prefer, was unaware of the fact that the Serbian army had been formed and that this zone was covered by the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's -- Madam Fauveau, you should rephrase it, because you are assuming that he -- this official, whoever the official would be, was unaware. I mean, I -- it takes me at least two to three weeks at the beginning of each year to get used to the idea of writing down the new year, and I keep writing the previous year. So I am perfectly aware that we would have started a new year, but it just happens that I keep writing down "2001" even though we are in 2002. It doesn't mean that I'm not aware. It means that -- it's just a habit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to interrupt. And I take the point that Ms. Fauveau is making about this document but in fact it seems to me that it ought to also be pointed out that they went on using the stamp of the 5th Corps after the transformation as well, which is clear from the document. So how good a point this is, I don't know. And we have spent a lot of time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I don't understand why the witness is being so -- when he could answer it in just two words or three words. Do you assume responsibility for what others write, Judge? Because I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar show the witness P740.1 and P740.2 -- 780.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects himself. 780.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, could you have a look at document P782, which is a decision of the judge from the municipal court in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say 78 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Because the interpretation says 782. And that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a decision from a judge of the municipal court in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at the Serbo-Croat version.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the case. That is the case. This is a document of the municipal court of Sanski Most, number 714/97, dated the 20th of October, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the Serbo-Croat version. It's on the first page, the second paragraph -- the last paragraph. And it's the second page in the English version. It's the only paragraph on that page. The judge of Sanski Most established that: [In English] "The son of the applicant was indeed killed on 25 June 1992 by Serb-Chetnik military units near the hospital in Kotor Varos." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: This terminology, "the Serbian Chetniks," is this a terminology -- are these terms that were currently used in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this is a derogative term for the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a derogatory term. It is one of pride for the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the "Ustasha" is also a term which is honourable for the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to move on to another subject. I need another 15 minutes. Would it be better to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have the break now. We'll resume in 30 minutes' time. So it's -- at five to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 13th of May -- page 48 of the LiveNote, it was from that point -- you stated what the procedure was in order to declare that a person who disappeared was dead. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that a birth certificate had to be attached to the request; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that normally -- in normal situations the municipality in which the person was born issues the birth certificate?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you document 780.1? It's a birth certificate. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the birth certificate of a person who was born in Kotor Varos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this birth certificate was issued by the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. This certificate was issued by an authority of the administration that was set up in the federation for citizens, refugees from the municipality of Kotor Varos; that is to say, their office, which had the authority to issue such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are right. And this organ, this office, did it have the archives of the Municipality of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so, because these offices for citizens who were refugees in the Federation had their own records, their books of registration, ledgers that they obtained from the authorities involved. But they did have these records of citizens. So they were established in the Federation for all municipalities, for all refugees in the Federation. For example, in Sanski Most, there were a few such offices: For the Municipality of Prijedor, for the Municipality of Banja Luka, for the Municipality of Kotor Varos, I think, then Bosanska Dubica, and other municipalities. I can't remember all these offices right now, but citizens who were staying as refugees in Sanski Most could address this office for the issuance of this kind of a document. So this is a legal document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the archives of Kotor Varos municipality remained in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. So the Municipality of Kotor Varos has its organs in Kotor Varos, and that is where the archives are.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did this office in Sanski Most have access to the archives in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I said that these offices had communications, some communications with these official institutions in Sarajevo, in the Federation, and they obtained these lists, these excerpts from the birth registers, because without this kind of an excerpt from the records of births, death, et cetera, they couldn't have issued documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about an identification number that every citizen in ex-Yugoslavia had. Do you remember speaking about this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you could confirm that all the citizens of ex-Yugoslavia had an identification number.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that fully, because a citizen would have to go to the authority in charge -- and that is public security station, or the MUP -- and then his personal identification number would have to be established. I don't know if all citizens had their personal identification numbers established. I assume they did. Not only the former Yugoslavia, but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina now, because a person who is of age, if he or she seeks to get an ID or a passport, has to have this personal identification number, just like children who are registered -- who are registered in these books of records.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the personal identification number consists of 13 figures?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the personal identification number consists of 13 figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the first seven figures in the personal identification number refer to the date of birth?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain why the birth certificate, which is P780.1, contains a personal identification number which is not complete and which only contains the numbers which refer to the date of birth? And I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that there is a translation error in the numbers in the English translation, in the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. There is an extra number, "9," which shouldn't be there. In fact, just for the record, the Trial Chamber is indicating that on the -- what appears to be the original, the identity number -- personal identity number is shown as 1505960, while in the translation -- translated version in English, the personal identity number is shown as 15095960, which does not correspond to the number shown on the original document. Yes. Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I had already noticed it, but I was going to -- to bring it up myself later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- can I just say that the only thing that I'm slightly concerned about is I understood -- and Your Honour will recall when I was going through the evidence of declarations of death and exhumations -- I understood there was no challenge to this evidence. And indeed both Defence counsel agreed. But we now seem to be going into -- we've already done it with part of the exhumations, how part of a body was identified and now with this particular birth certificate. If there is some kind of challenge, then obviously I'm going to have to devote more time to going through the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know whether there is a challenge or not, to tell you the truth, because I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite see where Madam Fauveau is heading. It may well be something much simpler, which I very much suspect, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] All right. Well, Your Honour, I'm just making that point so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Madam Fauveau, you may proceed for the time being as if this exchange of debate did not take place. Don't worry about it. Go ahead. If it's the case of drawing your attention to something, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain why this personal identification number is not complete?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that often records had shortcomings, in terms of personal identification numbers, because in the former Yugoslavia these records anyway were not complete, as far as personal identification numbers were concerned. I remember during the elections as well there were considerable difficulties concerning personal identification numbers. It is possible that this citizen did not have his personal identification number established. I don't know why it's missing. So it's this part, this date of birth. And the rest -- the rest can be established.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of which facts was a birth certificate issued in this Sanski Most office for the persons who were not born in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question now because I didn't go into records of these offices. But I would go and pay a visit to some of these offices, and I saw that they did have some records. You see what I'm saying? I really do not know on the basis of what this authority issued this certificate. I imagine that they had some records, some lists that they obtained from the central records of the MUP in Sarajevo or in some other way. But for me, this is a legal document concerning a person who was born in Kotor Varos with all the personal data contained here. This was confirmed by the person who actually initiated these proceedings before the court of law; that is to say, that these data are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this birth certificate was issued at the request of the family and that the facts weren't at all verified?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This certificate was issued upon the request of the family of the person concerned. As for the facts, I can't say anything about that. This was issued according to the procedure that was made possible for these authorities during the transition period after the war, because the citizens could not immediately address the authorities in Republika Srpska for the issuance of such documents. There were considerable difficulties. That is why these authorities, these offices, had been established as interim authorities. I think they've been abolished by now and that on the basis of federal regulation, such offices no longer exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 14th of May, you spoke about people in Vrhpolje who decided to not surrender their arms, their weapons, and to defend themselves. Do you remember speaking about this?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said -- and it's on page 17 of the LiveNote of the 14th of May -- that all these people were killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read what you stated. [In English] "They withdrew to a position above the village in order to defend their village, to defend their houses. They didn't want to surrender. They had infantry weapons on them. I think that all those people died. They were all killed."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from those who were involved in the exchange, I did mention that these persons had captured a group of officers and soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade and that they asked for an exchange and that this was made possible for them, that is, to take buses to a locality in Bihac. That's what I said. And there were about 180 such persons, perhaps a bit less. And the rest who stayed in the forest were captured and killed. Some were captured and interrogated at the public security station in Sanski Most, and there is a trace of that. There are statements, but all these persons were liquidated at an unknown locality. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you do agree that not all of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They all were not killed; that is to say, those who went to Bihac were not killed, those who were exchanged. And this was made possible for them. And I imagine that Mr. Talic knows this, that this group went to Bihac and that these 46 Serb officers and soldiers were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were 300 prisoners in Vrhpolje. Do you know how many of them were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure I gave was approximate, was less, I think. I said that this was the maximum that could have been there. According to what I know, 158 persons went to Bihac -- no, 183. 183. I received this information -- I received this information from persons who went to Bihac, and I saw them after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these resistance in Vrhpolje, these Muslims, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the extent to which they were armed, but I think that some of them - probably a large number - had small arms, light weapons. I mean automatic rifles, and some ammunition as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these people in Vrhpolje, these Muslim members of the resistance, were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that they wore uniforms. Possibly some of them could have had uniforms, but I don't know. I do not preclude that possibility, that somebody did have a uniform. But most of them had no uniforms. Most of them were in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So they were wearing civilian clothing and they had weapons. That's how it was, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure about that, so I really can't say. I know that there was one person who was a former JNA officer. He was with them and he was their commander and he was involved in negotiations with the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade concerning negotiations -- concerning an exchange. And he led these men.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you would allow for the possibility that some of these 300 Muslims in Vrhpolje, of these 300 resistance, were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing of the 15th of May, you spoke about mass graves in Vrhpolje, and you said that they weren't marked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: These mass graves were located in the vicinity of the bridge of Vrhpolje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some mass graves were right by the bridge and underneath the bridge at Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the bridge in Vrhpolje was destroyed in 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So these mass graves which were near or under the bridge in Vrhpolje were in a combat zone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which combat? Tell me, which combat? Conflicts took place in 1995. Are you referring to 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is possible that the markings at these mass graves were destroyed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not possible, because the ground where I was searching for the graves, it was levelled and there was grass there. There weren't any visible markings, because had there been any, people would have known that a grave was there and they would have marked that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When were these exhumations carried out, these exhumations in the vicinity of the Vrhpolje bridge?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several exhumations, because in that area several mass graves were found at several localities too. But over there by the bridge, the first exhumations were carried out, and there is a report in writing about that. I don't want to engage in guesswork concerning the date, et cetera, so I think it's there in the report. I can just say that I was informed by SFOR that they found this on the left-hand side while they were clearing the remnants of the bridge, that they found some skeletons deep down, and that they stopped further work on clearing the rubble, because they were supposed to build a bridge. That's when I established that particular locality. So it was SFOR that was the first to find this grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the year.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the beginning of 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this mass grave was beneath the debris of the bridge that had been destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So how can you say that among the debris from the bridge, there was no debris from markings of the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can assert that because people were there in September 1995, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No one told me that there was such a locality there. Furthermore, the grave was found deep down when they were digging there, because a new bridge was supposed to be built there. So it was not on the surface; it was deep down. This grave was concealed underneath the left side of the bridge by the river bank, by the bank of the River Sana.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that at the place where the mass grave was found, the terrain, the ground, had been covered by debris from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1996. Or rather, from October -- September 1995 until the bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have just one more question for you. Before you came to give testimony here, did you have the opportunity of reading the indictment against General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. Judge, you're now going to be cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman, do you prefer to take Madam Fauveau's place, or are you going to remain where -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Ackerman begins -- because effectively, Manjaca is more evidence-related to General Talic directly than Mr. Brdjanin. If I understand the cross-examination, part of a report has been read that said that conditions seemed to be all right and Mr. Ashdown's comments afterwards. There's been no specific challenge to any of the events and incidents that the judge described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, that in itself is a challenge, I think. No? It's -- in other words, I mean, his words are being put in question, in doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- By two affirmations coming from other sources. One was which supposedly Mr. Ashdown said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the other one Merhamet told the other gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes well, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I'm satisfied --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the reason I'm raising it at this stage so to make it very clear. Virtually every witness we're calling is going to be dealing with events in Manjaca. I'm anxious to reduce, if possible, the amount of time I have to spend with each witness dealing with the conditions in Manjaca. Obviously there will be two or three more -- if as I understand it, therefore, the challenge is limited to well, there are reports that say this was all right but that there's no -- because there is no -- Madam Fauveau has no specific instructions and cannot have specific instructions to challenge the detail, then I will take it that the general's defence on this is simply that he doesn't know one way or the other. It seems to me the proper way to draw it. Because otherwise, if there's more information specific to the detailed account of the camp that's been given by this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's put it like this. Ms. Korner -- and then I'll call upon you, Madam Fauveau, to make your remarks. The report that Madam Fauveau read from is very specific in that it relates to a period of four days --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those four days, however, supposedly representing an update of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But not an update on the report on the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Between the 16th and the 20th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically whatever that report states can only be referred to those particular four days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown's alleged comments -- because these are -- if I read well or I heard well, someone saying Mr. Ashdown said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, one actually hears him saying it in English at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date of Mr. Ashdown's visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically we're talking of the 10th of August and what he saw, what he was allowed to see, whatever. That's about it. Having said that, I now call upon you, Madam Fauveau, to remark or to comment on Ms. Korner's submission. In other words, what are you contesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I gave to the witness evidence that I had at the moment. In fact, what we are contesting is the image of this camp, and I didn't have any other evidence to show him other than the evidence that I presented him with. As far as the personal acquaintance with General Talic is concerned, Ms. Korner is quite right because General Talic never went to that camp, so it could only be based on the reports that he received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's -- that -- it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. Your Honour, that is clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman, if you're ready, we can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I am ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Draganovic, I have a lot of questions to ask you. I have 41 pages of notes of questions I want to ask you. And the Judge has told you that you can get yourself out of here quicker if you'll listen carefully to the question and just answer the question that I'm asking you and not follow that with some speech. Do you think you can do that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So do we all. You became a judge in Sanski Most, didn't you, in 1987?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it says in my statement exactly when I became a judge. It gives the exact date. It should be contained in my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you don't know when you became a judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't say that, Mr. Ackerman. He told you basically -- you already have the answer in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know when you became a judge?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my statement, it gives the date. And it was in 1997 -- no, not in 1997 -- in 1987 in Sanski Most. That's when I came from Bosanska Dubica, where I was also a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, we started this process with me suggesting to you that if you could just listen and answer my questions, we'd be a lot quicker. And the simple question I asked you is: You became a judge in Sanski Most in 1997? It would be so easy to say yes, rather than all this business about your statement, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Don't try to suggest to me how I should answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, you should know that if you are on a collision course -- and I am not going to help you. You are very much alone there. I have been a witness myself in my career. And as a judge, you are alone. As a witness, you are alone as well. And I can sense that if you are not careful, you are on a collision course. You could have answered the question in the simplest of ways, yes or no, and you didn't. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second thing you need to know, Mr. Draganovic, is your statements are not evidence in this case. The evidence in this case is the testimony you give from this witness stand and the exhibits that are admitted. So it is not sufficient to make evidence in this case that you said something in your statement. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you were not from Sanski Most. You were not born and raised, you didn't grow up in Sanski Most, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I grew up in Sanski Most, and I've lived in Sanski Most since when I was a child, but I was born in the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
