utterances.text: What I want to know is how is it that after only one year of going to the judiciary in Sanski Most, you were made the court president. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of regular procedure. That's how it happened. Since my term of -- the term of office of the former president had expired -- she was Snezana Tesanovic, I was proposed as the president of the court and I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And elected by whom?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was by the parliament. I was elected by the parliament -- or the Assembly of Sanski Most municipality. I can't remember now exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there other judges in Sanski Most that had been there longer than you in the lower court?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I don't think there were any other judges who had been there longer than myself. Perhaps one of the judges had been there for longer than I had, but she was on sick leave -- on maternity leave for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you became president, you'd been there about a year.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how is it you don't know who elected you judge? How could that be?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the laws had been changed. I know that the municipal courts were under the competence of the municipalities and that at sometime during that period, they fell under the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you -- as you sit here today, you just don't know who elected you president of that court.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most or the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the answer is you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told us in your testimony the other day that 48 members of your family had been killed during the war. Understand that I'm not asking you this question. I just am asking you: If I were to ask you to name each of these people and tell us how they died, would you be able to do that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- first of all, I didn't say 48. But I think that I could describe -- give the names of all my relatives who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told the Chamber a few moments ago -- well, let me ask you a question before I ask that one. The organisation Merhamet -- the organisation Merhamet is a Muslim charity organisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak humanitarian organisation. Yes, you could say that. But not just for Muslims; for everyone who needs help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that in 1992, it had offices in Banja Luka, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that Bosniaks worked in those offices and did the work of Merhamet during that year, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found out that they worked there. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know Adil Medic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you want to stand by your statement that Mr. Medic was under the control of Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement that Merhamet in Banja Luka was under the control of the Serbian authorities but not Adil Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that Adil Medic, on behalf of Merhamet, was visiting Manjaca, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On the first day of your testimony here, Mr. Draganovic, you told us -- I'm going to read you the exact question and answer. It's page 4846, lines 3 through 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Hmm?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 23 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Question: And you -- "And have you worked in liaison with the office of AID both in Sanski Most and in Sarajevo?" Answer: "Yes. I cooperated with the AID." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But he said much more than that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've read the entire answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could actually stay here and read the entire deposition as far as it relates to the questions that he was asked about his cooperation with AID, but I do remember that he said much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe during the cross-examination of Madam Fauveau he talked about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. It was not during the cross-examination only. Also on -- upon the cross-examination, but not only on cross-examination. Also on examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you want to look at page 4846, there is one question about AID and one answer about AID and that's it. There is nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, that may be on that particular date. But on other days he did amplify on the alleged cooperation with AID. So go straight to the question that you need to ask him, because it's not fair to refer the witness to one statement only if you know that he has made further statements on his cooperation with AID, be it on that same occasion or on other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know why you are saying his alleged cooperation with AID. It sounds like you have made a conclusion that he did not cooperate with AID --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the transcript he says he did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm saying "alleged" because it was put to him whether he cooperated or not, and it was put to him one way by one counsel and put to him in another way by another counsel. So when I say "alleged cooperation," because he's already qualified what kind of cooperation he had with the AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was put to him by the Prosecutor, "You worked in liaison with the office of AID both in Sanski Most and in Sarajevo," and his answer was yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then later he explained that he worked as a judge in cooperation with AID and he also worked not as a judge with AID. So this is why I am asking you go straight to the question that you want to ask him. Because he did explain in detail to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I object to your characterising it, Your Honour, as "alleged cooperation." That sounds like a finding being made by the Court that he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I can assure you that it is no finding at all, especially knowing that you are going to ask questions to the witness on his cooperation with AID. He has already stated that he cooperated, but it's not the cooperation that was put to him at one point in time. He qualified his cooperation by explaining what kind of cooperation it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you prior to coming here to testify in the period of time between the time you knew you would be a witness in this case and the time you came here to testify, did you speak with anyone from AID about the testimony you would give here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Could you repeat that question again. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that period of time between the time you became aware that you would be a witness in this case and when you actually came here to The Hague, did you speak with anyone from AID about your testimony, about the testimony you would give here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that period of time that you returned home while we had a break in the trial, did you speak with anyone there, AID or otherwise, about your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In Sanski Most during the investigations you conducted in 1995 and later, you knew a person by the name of Zijad Ibric, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he worked for AID, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do I have to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know the answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Zijad Ibric worked for AID, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zijad Ibric does work for the AID. He's an official in AID, the Agency for Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anybody from AID give you a ride to the airport in your trips here?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never. I don't drive around with those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You think that would be improper, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think anything. I know who -- who brought me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You and Mr. Zijad Ibric interviewed some witnesses together, didn't you, in connection with those investigations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as an example, sir, I'd like you to look at three exhibits, DB73.1, DB74.1, and DB76.1. I'd ask you be shown those, please. Now, sir, my question is really very simple, and I think it would be very easy for you to answer it. All I want to do is direct you to the last page of each of those statements and ask you if it's not the case that these documents show that you and Zijad Ibric took statements from the person whose name also appears -- and signature also appears on those documents. And I'm only showing you it for that purpose. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statement that I took as an investigating judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Referring to 73.1? Just look at all of them and then confirm for me that they're all statements that you took as investigating judge, along with Zijad Ibric.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this statement as an investigating judge, and Mr. Zijad Ibric typed this statement out on a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you're referring to 73. what? Look at the front. It says 73. something on it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 73.1? Now, look at 73.2. The same thing? It should say DB73.1, DB73.2 -- no, 74.1 and DB76.1.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Take the first one of these documents, DB73.1, please, Judge. Starting from the title [B/C/S spoken], and skip the first paragraph, consisting of one line, the second paragraph, consisting of eight lines. The third paragraph, starting with [B/C/S spoken]. Can you read out that paragraph so that I have it translated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "This statement is being taken and recorded by the investigating judge of this court, Adil Draganovic, with the assistance of an official from the AID, Zijad Ibric."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two copies are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Give me the numbers of the identical ones.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this one. Down here there is a Prosecution number, 00431945, and number 00431945. They are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're correct. I think two of them are identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In the first of these documents, you have a reference number which is redacted, while in the second you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe they're identical, Your Honour. They were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. If it's not important for you, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- You may go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My only purpose, sir, in showing you these was to show that you and Mr. Ibric worked together in taking these statements. And you signed them yourself, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's how this statement was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about a man named Husein Ganic? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall if you and Mr. Ibric took a statement from a gentleman named Husein Ganic? Does that ring any bells with you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to bring to your attention and move the admission of defendant Brdjanin Exhibit number 77. I will tell you that it is a -- an extract from the transcript in the Kvocka case, pages 11018 through 11060. It contains --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Through 11060. Those are the page numbers of transcript. It contains the full testimony--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour. I object to this completely. I object to a description of this document. I object to the admission of testimony from another case which the Defence, if they wish to put it in and it has some relevance -- I was unaware till this morning. Indeed a pile of documents was placed on the -- in front of me this morning, which I haven't had an opportunity to go through, and I object to this in its entirety. And if this is going to happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is something which I had hoped we agreed upon in the very beginning of this trial. And this is somewhere where cooperation has been shortcoming, because it's not fair that even the Chamber itself comes to today's sitting only knowing what documents are -- you're going to make use of at the beginning of the sitting, at 9.00, and then having the documents available during the first -- first break and not having had an opportunity to go through them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not what we had agreed upon in the very beginning of this trial, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The same applies to Madam Fauveau. And sometimes the same applies to you, because you do exactly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And my complaint is quite a clear one. You should not -- I do acknowledge that everyone is busy here, but I do acknowledge also that we have an agreement that you should make available the documentation or at least indicate what documents you are going to make use of in good time. I don't expect to know weeks and months before, but at least we should be in a position to know a day before what documents you are going to make use of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not in fact correct. Unless Your Honour points to a specific incident in each case. Because otherwise there's complaints from the Defence. We say the documents we're going to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, there have been days when I came here having a List of Documents which I had asked my staff to have prepared for me and I have gone through only to find out that in the space of 12 hours, that list has changed, it has increased in number. That happened yesterday. For example, Madam Fauveau started with a list of about six or seven documents. All of a sudden yesterday I found out that -- or the day before yesterday that it had increased in number, multiplied by about three or four. And as regards your list, we only had it this morning, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we return -- I'm sorry if Your Honour feels that we're deficient in providing lists. As I've said, in fact, we're not going provide lists in future because it's too complicated. We're going to hand out the documents was we come to them. But Your Honour, at this moment; we've drifted slightly off the point, which is I was unaware that an attempt was going to be made to put in part of a transcript, and I certainly want to read it and in principle I object to method -- this method of attempting to adduce evidence into a trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't read it either, Ms. Korner. The only thing I can suggest at this point in time -- banking on the cooperation of -- from Mr. Ackerman -- is if he could postpone this -- putting this question with regard to that -- to later until we at least go through the script -- the transcript and see what it is -- what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we will decide on your objection later on, because I -- don't expect me to rule on the admissibility of this document and on the -- the legitimacy of the question that Mr. Ackerman has put and will be putting on this document, not having read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just say that it represents prior recorded testimony that the Prosecutor had --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I object to this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't -- don't say it in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I object --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not going to talk about the content at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what's the prior recorded testimony got to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I object to this. I don't want any of the content of this document -- until I have had a chance to look at it. And Your Honour, I would in future ask that if this type of document is -- there's going to be attempt to put it in, we must be notified in advance so we don't have this unseemly discussion in front of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave it at that for the time being. We are going to take time to read this document. And there is Mr. Ackerman's understanding on this. He will put the question if it's admitted -- and the document-- on the document if it's admitted later on. Is that okay with you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person by the name of Jasminka Putica?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it -- let me see if I can refresh your memory a bit. She is a judge in Sarajevo. Do you know her?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have I got the name wrong?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the name is.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking about a judge, I know that there is a judge by the name of Jasminka Putica at the Supreme Court of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I thought I said. Obviously I was misunderstood. And do you know what her ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman by the name of Bakir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Bakir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you heard of him in connection with any function that he had with AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that he used to be the chief of AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read about that in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where he is now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you read in the newspapers that he's in jail?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Enver Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about Irfan Ljevakovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Irfan Ljevakovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Edhem Veladzic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to Edhem Veladzic, I do know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know him -- he was the ex-chief of police security centre in Bihac. Is that where you knew him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him as former minister of the police of the canton of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where he is now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Didn't you read that he was in jail?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read about it, because I've been in The Hague for a long while now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us that you had read something in the newspaper about Mr. Alispahic that had to do with some of his recent problems, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're driving at, but -- I really don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about -- do you know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm going to ask what the relevance of this is. What this witness may or may not have read about people in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be happy to tell you out of the presence of the witness. I'd be eager to tell you out of the presence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the microphone. Usher, could you escort the witness out for a while, and then we'll continue. Judge, we need to discuss something in your absence, which I am sure you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] He doesn't need to be taken far, because I suppose this is only going to last a couple of minutes. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can tell you only my current understanding, and I can also tell you this matter is -- continues to be under investigation. But it is clear that five individuals have been arrested and are sitting in jail in Sarajevo, having been detained on the orders of this judge Jasminka Putica. They are described as five former officials of AID and their associates, including the former head of AID, Mr. Alispahic. They are charged by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina with engaging in terrorist activities, with manufacturing documents. And it's a very, very serious matter. There is an article about it in Oslobodenje. And I have an investigation going on trying to find out more about it. They apparently also were engaged in some kind of a plot to assassinate Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was the person who got the most votes in the election for president of BiH but was not seated. Mr. Izetbegovic was seated instead. So Abdic went off to the Bihac area and formed his own organisation and actually wound up fighting against the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces, the Bosnian army. He's a controversial figure. He was recently tried, as I understand it, in Croatia. And as I understand it -- and please understand my information right now is pretty sparse -- the purpose of this plot to kill him was that he was seen by these people at AID as a traitor to their cause, which is -- well, I'm not going to describe what it is because I want to investigate a little further. But I think it's a serious matter. I only wanted to ask this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- If these were people he had worked with. And apparently they are not. So that will end my questions to him. This matter will come to your attention I think in much greater detail at some point regarding all the documents we have here from AID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. At this point I think the questions that he's been putting up, perfectly legitimate, providing he ends the question there, depending on what kind of answer he gets.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask again. How is it relevant that certain people that this witness may or may not know have been arrested and charged?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But again, these are allegations, like -- like I said. It -- I am taking them on the face value for the time being. I take Mr. Ackerman's word that the facts are as he states, as he stated -- in other words, that proceedings have been instituted against these four or five persons. Obviously -- I mean, he's got an interest to establish whether the witness ever cooperated or worked with these four or five persons in particular if amongst the charges that they are facing is the fabrication of false -- forged documents, as he has suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. At the moment, Mr. Ackerman may be right, he may be wrong. I haven't the faintest idea even if Your Honour hasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we are not judging --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I finish, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am simply asking what is the relevance unless it is suggested that a particular document that we have produced -- and I've been through this before. We've had these wild allegations being made. If it is suggested that these particular documents, any one of them that we have got, are forged, are not authentic, then that -- and that this witness knows something about it, then it can be put. But this sort of general do you know these people and then Your Honour to be informed that these people have been arrested and have been charged and the charges involved -- Your Honour, again, I say what is the relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must respond, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I'm going to exempt you from having to respond, Mr. Ackerman, because the position is as follows: The Chamber has admitted on a prima facie basis all the documents -- practically all the documents that you brought forward, knowing all the time that there is a ongoing objection on the part of both Mr. Ackerman and Madam Fauveau with regard to if not all, the majority of documents originating from Bihac and in the case of Madam Fauveau in particular, documents originating from Sarajevo. We've had statements in this Chamber that these documents are not trusted. Now, obviously the question is still there at the end of the day. That's going to be one of our major tasks. We will have to distinguish between one document and another and come to a conclusion. At this point in time, if there is this allegation throughout -- permeating all the proceedings in this case that some documents which are unsigned or unstamped or both and some documents originating from Sarajevo and some documents originating from AID and -- and/or Bihac, these are being contested -- although for the time being, no specific details are forthcoming with regard to any one of these particular documents. If there is an allegation now or if there is a statement by Mr. Ackerman that there are persons from AID that are being charged with -- amongst inter alia fabrication of documents, I'm going to allow to question, to see whether the judge -- whether the witness has ever been associated with these five persons, because that may have a relevance. If he has been associated with these five persons, that may -- it may not have a relevance even if he has been associated, because everything stands to be proved. But if he has not been associated in any way with these five persons, obviously that is going to be given its due weight. If he has been associated with these five persons, that will also be given its due weight. This is why I'm definitely going to allow the question to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, I'm not going to pursue this -- I'm not going to pursue except to point out to Your Honour that the fact that these people may have been arrested, may have been charged, proves precisely nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the allegation is -- and I repeat this again and then I'm going to sit down, Your Honour -- that a particular document or all the documents in this case that come from -- through the auspices of AID are forged, fine, then let that be put and we'll deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That stands to be seen and to be decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. Your Honour. But that's why I need to deal with that. Obviously, if that's the allegation that's been made and it's going to be put in terms that any documents handed in through this witness who allege -- who says, I'm sorry, not alleges -- who says he found these documents in the CSB that these documents were not found there, or that they've been forged by him in conjunction with other members of the AID, then that is an allegation that must been put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait one moment. Ms. Korner, the motion is very simple in any mind, at least. It's true that what Mr. Ackerman has stated as being reported -- and I don't know which newspaper -- is something that is -- seems to be in the air, that one day or another maybe will be decided but that at the present moment there is no decision on those facts. But do you expect the Trial Chamber to ignore as if it is not happening the fact that there are four or five persons from AID that are being charged -- I'm not saying that they are guilty -- but that are being charged with, amongst other things, fabrication of documents, when this Trial Chamber has in front of it an allegation from the Defence, again which will need to be decided upon later on, that there are amongst the documents originating from Sarajevo or -- and AID documents that are forged or are not being accepted? How can I ignore that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think I'll answer Your Honour's question. Thank you. I've made my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, if there's anything that you would like to say, please go ahead. If not, we'll get the witness back, and I would like you to put the question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm not sure I have a question left to put. I think I went through every individual. Let me just make sure. I think I -- the last person I asked him about was Mr. Alispahic and he said he didn't know him. And that was the end of the names. And I don't think there's another question to put to him because he doesn't know them and he clearly doesn't work with them. And that would end it. But let me say this: Ms. Korner is trying to shift a burden to us that we cannot have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not going to be shifted to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what she's saying is we must show they're forgeries. She must show they're authentic. And by Your Honour's ruling at the beginning of this trial if we raise any indication whatsoever that these documents do not come from an official source and are not trustworthy, then it's up to the Prosecutor to prove their authenticity. That's her job, not ours. It's not our job to prove they are forgeries. So she has her burdens wrong. She has what she has to do wrong. Secondly, I have newspaper articles that say more about this, but they say things that I think might be reckless. For instance, they connect these people with Al Qaeda and the activities of Al Qaeda in the U.S. And I don't think -- that may not be responsible. The one newspaper that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have enough on our shoulders already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The responsible newspaper of Oslobodenje. It's not a Serbian newspaper. It's an independent newspaper. And the charges are made by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not Serbian court. And so that's all I have to say about it. And so say that this is wild allegations, I think is -- is an outrageous thing for her to say. If the Prosecutor knew about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They could be the wildest of allegations. I don't care at this point in time, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the Prosecutor knew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a hint that there may be -- there could have been cooperation between any witness -- not just this one -- and AID members or officials who are being charged -- presently charged with fabrication of documents, that is of course of interest to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I want to say is if the Prosecutor knew about it, I think it was her obligation to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor didn't know about it. I mean, don't bring it -- as if the Prosecutor knew about this and is trying to hide something from us. I mean, I don't take it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know nothing whatsoever about this. I will clearly be making inquiries as a result of now finally being told. Had we been asked about this, we could have probably made inquiries ourselves. But the point is still -- the one I made is in our submission a valid one. Of course the burden is upon us to show that these documents are authentic. Not for one moment do I suggest that the Defence has any burden upon it to show they're not authentic. But if the suggestion is going to be made that all the documents that we have produced, that come through the auspices of AID are in some way suspect or forged, then of course we will discharge our burden by calling as much evidence as we can to show that those documents are in fact authentic. But until such time as we have an inkling -- because this is the first time it's been suggested -- or at the beginning of this trial that these documents are forgeries -- we can't discharge our burden unless we know about it. So that's all that I'm saying about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Perfectly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The second thing is, Your Honour, as I say again in respect of this witness, if the suggestion is to be made because he has cooperated with AID officials, he in some way is responsible for the creation or has lied about documents, then that must be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right there as well. I think we can leave it at that for the time being. We'll have a break. Madam Registrar, please, the witness will be taken to his room. And until he continues with his evidence in 30 minutes' time, he must remain incommunicado. That includes members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait. We don't have the accused present as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Ackerman continues, it may be as well if we were to leave ten minutes at the end of the session to deal with the document which I've now read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, you have read it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I read it on the break. I know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it will take longer. And also there's a couple of administrative matters I want to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So we'll agree, Mr. Ackerman -- I would say we stop at least ten minutes before quarter to 2.00 so that we thrash this -- the submission on this document and whatever is left to be discussed. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing is what I'm told was a mistranslation. That document 73.1, Your Honour, that you asked the witness to read, the third paragraph of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm told by my associates that that was not properly translated, and I'm wondering how you would like to try to solve that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I can solve that problem by kindly asking you to turn to your co-counsel who knows the language, and if she agrees to read that third paragraph, if I remember well. Then we -- I'm not going to ask the witness again to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slowly. Slowly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RADOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The statement was taken and recorded by the investigating judge of this court, Adil Draganovic with the cooperation of Ibric Zijad a professional associate of the AID -- a professional official from the AID." [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy now with the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I suppose I am. Your Honour. I was just told that the original one was not absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you may proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I'd like the witness to be given DB78, please. And Your Honour -- oh, Your Honour, I mentioned to Ms. Korner that there actually was one lingering question from what we were doing right before the break, and that's what I'm going to do now. It will be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I would suppose it's expected from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you did recognise the name Edhem Veladzic as being someone who had served as a minister in Bihac. And I've now given you two -- one document, which actually contains two documents, DB78 B. And you'll notice two signatures, a signature on each of those documents, purporting to be from a person Edhem Veladzic. Is that the person that you were talking about that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is this a person that you ever worked closely with in connection with your work with AID?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This person has nothing to do with my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I know you have told us this, and I'm asking you again simply because I don't recall. What -- when was it -- the date that you returned to Sanski Most in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think you told us that that was about five days after the army had captured Sanski Most, the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was Sanski Most like five days after the BiH army retook it? What did you see when you returned to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived there in the afternoon with my wife. I first went to see my house which had been destroyed. I went there. It was a sunny afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were there a lot of military vehicles in the streets?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How about flags and symbols of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering. I'm just asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just answer the question. I mean, it's -- why do you want to argue the point? He might as well ask you why there were other flags. But what's the point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there were flags in front of the municipality building. I don't know whether there were any others. I saw some flags, but only the flags of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you immediately upon your return -- I mean, within a day or two, resume your post as president of the court?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first few days, I had conversations in the municipality building, and I then went to the court building and prepared to resume my work in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did some authority ask you to resume your post as president of the court, or did you just do that on your own authority?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I first heard that another colleague of mine who was a lawyer had been appointed as the president of the court in Sanski Most. Knowing full well that he couldn't have that post and that the organs in Sanski Most could not do that, I went and told them that I had come there to carry on with my work, and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the colleague who had been appointed president I take it was someone who had been appointed by the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who had appointed this person?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidency of the municipality had appointed him before I arrived there from Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Ismet Sarcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how was it you took over his position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the president of the presidency, who was then Mr. Mirzet Karabeg, and to Alagic Mehmed, who was a member of that presidency. And I spoke to them. I explained that I had come to stay and to start with my work and that I was a legal -- president of the court in Sanski Most and the judge and that no one else could be appointed to this position without following the procedure, and they agreed with me on that point. I then went to the building of the municipal court, where I met Mr. Sarcevic, and he really showed me the decision of the presidency according to which they were appointing him as president of the court. I explained to the gentleman that that could not stand, that there was a legal procedure that had to be followed, and that my term of office had not yet expired, and I asked him to leave the building immediately. He handed over the keys to me without objecting, and he left the building, and he no longer attempted to get involved in my work. And on my own initiative, I started working at that point, because according to the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, my term of office had not yet expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long was your term of office?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my term of office was four years as president of the court. But as a judge, the term of office was for an eight-year period. But given the wartime situation, an amendment had been made to the law, and these terms of office had been extended until further notice and they were valid for six months after the end of the war. Or that is to say, after the signing of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So did Ismet Sarcevic remain as a judge of the lower court even though he was not the president?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, he left the building, and he stopped doing this work. He didn't do anything else. He was a deputy of the head of the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to assume that he was not happy with what you did?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't show this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he didn't send you a bouquet of flowers either, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did other judges who had left in 1991/1992 return and resume their positions in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were the only one that came back and resumed your position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume there came a time when you started living in your house in Mahala again. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three years later, when I had managed to repair it to a certain extent and ensure that there were living conditions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the repairs you made was to replace the roof, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The roof was replaced too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how did you do that? Where did you get the materials to replace the roof?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a labourer who had built a roof for me before, I agreed that he should repair the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But my question was: Where did the materials come from? Where did the actual roof come from that was put on your house?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This labourer obtained the material -- or rather, he and his relatives obtained the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know from where?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what would the answer be?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, please don't take my place. I'm the Judge here. You are the witness. For the time being, you have to answer that question, until I am not of the opinion that it is an irrelevant question that is being asked, you are required to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to explain for the time being, Mr. Ackerman. Put the question again, and the witness will answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If what I thought to be the case is actually the case, it may be that -- the reason I'm hesitating is I'm hesitating as to whether I want to say this to you in the presence of the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't, we'll send the witness out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's better we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Looking at the time, is there much -- I wonder if Mr. Ackerman perhaps could move to another topic and then he could deal with that when we're going to deal with the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't, if I were you. I would -- I would rather the witness leaves the courtroom for a while. Is it going to take you long to put this to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It will be extremely brief. Probably less than one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the witness is better out rather than in, if this is going to be discussed. Also because he's being reticent, he doesn't want to answer the question. So that makes me suspicious in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, my point is it's going to leave ten minutes -- by the time he goes out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I want this to be done and concluded before the witness goes back the his hotel. I have my own reasons. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information I have -- which is not completely verified. I understand there is even a videotape -- is that the roof that is on his house was stolen from a home of a Serb resident who had left the area because the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had taken it over, that he and his workers went there and stole the roof off that house and took it over and put it on his. The reason I hesitated to have him answer the question when he said what he said was it became clear to me that that may be the case. And in that case, it may be that you should advise him that -- of his rights regarding self-incrimination, because it may be a crime what he did, if that's what he did. And that's why I wanted to do it out of his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The witness can -- the usher is with him. No? Okay. You can bring the witness in again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge, I am -- I am authorising Mr. Ackerman to put the question to you again. In other words, as to whether you knew where the material for the construction of the roof or reconstruction of the roof came from. If in answering that question you think that you may be throwing some -- you would be giving some information which could be either incriminating or that you have a good reason not to answer, then you can ask for the permission of the Trial Chamber not to answer the question. But you have to furnish an explanation first. Mr. Ackerman, you may proceed with the question, and then we'll deal with it as -- with the problem as we go along. It's not being hinted that you have anything that is incriminating. But it's not being excluded either. In other words, I will have to answer -- ask -- wait for the question and for your answer, and we'll move from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question, sir, is: Where did the materials come from that you used to replace your roof?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an arrangement, an agreement with the labourer with regard to obtaining the materials for the roof, with the labourer who worked on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you knew where the labourer got those materials. The question is: Where did the materials come from?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The labourer said that this was second-hand material that he had collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why were you hesitant to answer that question when I first asked you? Why did you feel you should not answer it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just think that this is not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, sir, that you know that that material came from the roof of the home of a Serb resident who had left Sanski Most when the BiH army came there? It was stolen from that residence and put on your house; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you want to break now, Your Honour, or do you want me to go forward?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you have no further questions that you can bring to an end in five minutes, we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do. I can do five more minutes, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would ten minutes be sufficient for what you have to exchange?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No idea, Your Honour. I wouldn't have thought it should take longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll go on for the next five minutes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long after your return to Sanski Most did you begin conducting investigations?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already said that in my statement, that I started collecting documents straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you doing those -- this document collection that you were doing, were you doing that as a judge of the lower court of Sanski Most, or was that something you were doing as a private individual?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do anything as a private individual, only as a judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this gathering of documents, then, I take it was in connection with some case that was being put together in your court to charge someone with a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to duty by the presidency of the municipality to collect documents and evidence concerning war crimes in the territory of the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has -- he has already explained this, Mr. Ackerman, with reference to the document itself or two documents, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How is it that the presidency of the municipality was in a position to control the court and to tell the president of the court what to do? How is that? I thought you were independent.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But since there were quite a few documents and at that time it was necessary to tour various institutions and have a look at these documents. This was suggested to me, and I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you characterise it as a suggestion that you accept it rather than any order from the president of the municipality; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It was not an instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did anyone else direct your investigations and tell you what to investigate or suggest to you what to investigate, or did you do most of this on your own?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not a classical investigation. This was collection of evidence, facts, documents. And they were submitted to prosecution authorities. At that time, as a professional man and in cooperation with the cantonal prosecutor's office in Bihac, I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if the witness has more answer to my question, I guess he can give it in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The witness can be escorted out. Thank you, Judge. We'll continue tomorrow. Do you think you will finish your cross-examination tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will try very hard, Your Honour. I'm on page 8 of a 41-page set of notes. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness is being pretty short in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we're going to get there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Reply. So if I can ask you to make an effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll certainly make an effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge, you may withdraw. Thank you. And we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this refers back -- Your Honour, this refers back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: DB77.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. DB77. But it refers back to what Madam Fauveau was attempting to do in her cross-examination relating to the Kvocka trial, to which I object. Your Honour, there are really two objections, but I don't have to go further than relevance. It's the transcript of a graphologist who gave evidence on behalf of the Defence in respect of a statement taken by AID from a witness who in fact was granted protective measures. So I'm not going to refer to his name -- suggesting that the signature on the statement taken by AID was in fact not the signature of the man who purported to sign it. Your Honour, this was not a witness that we're calling. This is not a statement referred to which there is any suggestion that this witness had anything to do with it. The fact that it was alleged by the Defence and it got no further than an allegation that Mr. Ibric in some way forged that signature. It was never ruled upon because in the event it didn't need to is neither here nor there as far as this trial is concerned nor as far as this witness is concerned. In any event, this is not the way to attempt to get in evidence that relates to a person who is not a witness to the case. Your Honour, that's very simply my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, before you reply to this, given what the witness has already testified on, his connections or absence of them with the four -- five persons that you mentioned and also as to the names -- other names that you mentioned, I would like you to address also the relevance of this document when you are replying, because that's important. I mean, I haven't read it. I don't know whose signature was in question in this other case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you don't need to read it in detail. It was -- it was a witness in the other case who's not a witness in this case, who gave evidence, actually. And it was suggested apparently on behalf of the Defence that Mr. Ibric from AID in the statement he had taken from this witness -- the only relevance of which can have been contradictory -- can I just finish, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had forged the witness's signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I remember when Madam Fauveau had raised the matter, the -- her intention was to ask the witness whether he knew --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- About this incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And again I say it's irrelevant whether he knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I see you standing, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. You are -- you interpreted my question quite correctly. And in fact, I didn't continue to pursue this line of questioning because the witness replied no. I don't really see how Ms. Korner can say that it is a question which is not relevant since if the witness knew anything about this incident, he could have told us what the working methods of the AID were. And as Ms. Korner says, there are many documents which come from the AID which we contest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Given the situation or the picture as it emerges, Mr. Ackerman, what's your position? Are you going to proceed with questioning the witness on this document, or are you going to limit it to the -- to some other simple question without the need of having to refer or -- to this document or bring it -- or seek to bring it in evidence -- tender it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I want to do at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll explain to you why. Because if you see that you are not going to get anything from the witness on this document, we will visit the problem when it comes to the evidence that will be tendered by the -- by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not finished with Mr. Zijad Ibric, so any judgement made about whether this is relevant or not, based on the proposition that I am finished with Zijad Ibric would be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know whether you are or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I suggest to you is that we defer whether or not this document is admissible until I've finished my cross-examination and then perhaps you'll see that it is. The question, of course, has to do with this witness's association with and working with Zijad Ibric who this piece of transcript shows may very well have forged the signature of a witness to a statement. Ms. Korner tells you that witness was protected. But you will see if you look at the statement that his name is openly mentioned throughout the testimony. So if he was protected, at least his name was not protected. And Ms. Korner says you don't have to read it. And of course you do. I mean, if you're going to determine its admissibility, you do have to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will read it for sure. You can rest assured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think the best thing is to wait until I have finished all the questions I'm going to ask him about Ibric and all the things I'm going to do about Ibric before I then submit it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I better make this absolutely clear. Your Honour said, "Are you going to ask the witness about it?" I object to the witness being asked about testimony in other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. No. What I suggested was asking the witness questions that may actually originate from here but without making it explicit that he's being asked or without reading out to him or without having in evidence the transcript of proceedings in another case. I mean, he could -- for example, what Madam Fauveau was seeking was to ask the witness whether he knew a certain person, first; and secondly, whether he knew that the signature of that certain person had been forged or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, that's not what she asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. What she --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She didn't ask the question. She was seeking to ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She was seeking to ask, Your Honour - I know she'll correct me if I'm wrong - not whether the witness whose signature was forged knew about it. She was seeking to ask whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the witness knew that there had been an allegation made in the Kvoca case that he, Mr. Ibric, had forged somebody's signature. That's what she asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's objectionable on any grounds, because it's irrelevant. If the question had been phrased "At the time when you were collecting evidence together with Mr. Ibric or taking statements, were you aware -- did you know that he was in the habit of forging signatures," fine. Although, there's no evidence of that. But nonetheless, the way it was phrased was objectionable. And I see both counsel on their feet. They'll have a chance when I'm finished. What I'm saying is this is not a proper way of getting this sort of evidence in. And certainly the admission of a transcript of an examination and cross-examination of a graphologist relating to a statement not before this Court -- to a witness not before this Court is irrelevant and objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman first -- or rather, I would give the floor to Madam Fauveau, because obviously her remark would be shorter and related only to -- Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I still don't understand the objection raised by Mrs. Korner. My question was exactly what you said and what Mrs. Korner said. It's not a witness who has no relation to this Tribunal. It's a witness who has been cooperating with this Tribunal for years. And it concerns a trial which has a direct connection with the investigations carried out by this witness in Bosnia and also a connection with the trial that is being conducted here. And I can't ask this witness whether the signature of the person in question is false or not because I have no evidence with regard to this. The only thing that I can ask is what I did ask, whether -- when in his contact with the Prosecutor or with others, was he -- did he hear that there was an allegation about a signature on a document from AID, an allegation that this was a false signature. And I don't see why this should be inappropriate in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a very simple approach to it. You asked the witness with regard to the documents that he has been shown where there are three signatures -- his own, the AID man - I forgot his name - and the person making the statement -- whether that person put his signature in his presence. And that would bring everything to an end. Mr. Ackerman, with regard to those three documents -- or two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the names that I asked this witness today if he recalled was the name of the witness whose name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- you see in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I have information that he was involved in the taking of that statement and that his signature appears on it. The problem is this: The report of the expert and the forged document are missing from the records of this court. We tried to get them. We were told that they're gone. Now, if I were a particularly paranoid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were told by this Chamber that they were gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We were told by the Registry that they were gone. Now, if I were a particularly suspicious and paranoid individual, I would wonder if that didn't happen to protect AID and Mr. Ibric. But I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to state that this document was ever in -- amongst the documents that you tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. No. They were exhibits in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the Kvocka case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do we have to do with that? I mean -- I mean, I thought you had asked Madam Registrar to give you this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: . No, no, no. I'm not suggesting you had anything to do with it. We were trying to confirm what we heard about this witness's signature also appearing on the document, and we wanted to look at the actual report of the witness so we could be a little bit more precise about what we're doing here. And we're told those documents are all missing. And that's the word I think that was used, isn't it, that they were missing? It's missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I could even add that the document in question is D28/4 and D29/4 in the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've run over time, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we'll have to -- I've made my objection. And Mr. Ackerman says he wants to deal with it at the end of his cross-examination, so let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just very quickly just ask -- we're just finishing off the protective measures motion for the rest of the witnesses. It will run over. The page limit is ten pages for a motion. Can we -- it's so obvious. Your Honours asked us to do it. Can we have leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's necessary. If it's necessary, you have our consent -- our authorisation straight away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Your Honour while I'm here -- and finally very quickly, in relation to Rule 92 for Sanski Most, the two witnesses who Your Honour ruled that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- need to be brought for cross-examination, no protective measures - that's Mr. Kurbegovic and Mr. Seferovic - we're not going to extend the life of the Sanski Most thing by calling them, so we're not going to call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's -- in respect of Mr. Mayhew, we're going to see what the cross-examination in respect of Mr. MacLeod is like before we decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. My apologies --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if you've ordered that they be brought here by cross-examination, is it up to the Prosecutor whether to comply with that order or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you've ordered that these witnesses be brought here for cross-examination, is it the Prosecutor's decision as to whether or not to comply with your order?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- we're going to get slaughtered by the Samac case, but Your Honour, in fact we asked -- we said we want to put the evidence in under Rule 92 and we didn't want to call them. Your Honours said no, if we want to put them in under Rule 92, we have to have them here for cross-examination. We're saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't think you need to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it's -- to me, it's very clear. That's why I asked Mr. Ackerman to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's too late in the day. I'm sorry. I shouldn't have even raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So my apologies again to the technical staff and to the interpreters. You've been most kind. I thank you. Tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
